extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; writers and orators interested in personal essay and speech practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and self-prescriptive remarks on composing and presenting personal essays and orations, including authorial stances on revision, memory, style, and editorial handling. Primarily a 16th‑century essayist's reflections on how to write and speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add but correct not (editing/publishing principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a man having parted with his labours to the world has no further right to them; the author grants liberty to add small new emblems on new editions, but will not 'adulterate' what he has already sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne permits additions on new editions to give 'particular value' but warns against altering the original work's primitive form. He accepts some transposition of chronology (stories placed by opportuneness) but resists substantive rewriting of previously published pieces: 'I add, but I correct not.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive revision and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition is troublesome and ruinous in matters with only a superficial and transitory show; the author dislikes over-insisting (as in Seneca) and prefers not to restate common universal reasons at full length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises the stoical habit of reiterating principles at great length; he warns that repeating what is already said burdens the reader and diminishes value. He expresses fear of unintentionally repeating himself across works and of writing the same thought twice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on memory or premeditation for speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying wholly on memory or preparing studied speeches undermines natural delivery and the speaker's composure; premeditation makes one lose power and appear artificial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: Lyncestes' prepared speech failed him and was taken as a confession; Curio's enumerated parts led to forgetting items. Montaigne prefers 'casual and unpremeditated motions' and values the calmness of present invention over heavy rehearsed orations: 'The preparation begets a great deal more expectation than it will satisfy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid enumerated promises and rigidly divided orations
rubrics_metrics.description: Promising to divide an oration into numbered parts or prescribing a set structure invites failure (forgetting, adding) and relishes too much of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne reports that setting out 'three or four parts' often causes the speaker to forget or to add more, and he hates such promises and prescriptions because they betray craft over natural expression. He prefers simplicity to formal, counted structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplicity in expression and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity is preferable to overt artifice in speech and demeanor; 'Simpliciora militares decent'—simplicity becomes soldiers (i.e., suits those who are natural and direct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne deprecates an overly 'artist' manner in public speaking and values plain, unpretentious delivery. He suggests that simplicity prevents expectation-driven disappointment and fits better with a calm, present invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthography and punctuation secondary; author disclaims responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The author is unconcerned with orthography and pointing, acknowledging inexpertise; he will not obsess over such mechanics except where they wholly break sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne states he 'neither concern[s] myself with orthography ... nor pointing,' and accepts faults of workmanship where they do not destroy meaning. This is an explicit tolerance for mechanical errors in favour of preserving the author's voice/content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject spurious or misattributed sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: When an editorial reading produces a sentence not strong enough for the author's proportion, a courteous reader should reject it as spurious and not ascribe it to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne asks that readers/editorial hands not force meanings onto him by changing text: where a revision substitutes a false sense it 'ruins' him. He advises civility in rejecting sentences that do not match his voice or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid binding promises; voluntary actions have more grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done voluntarily have grace and honour that compelled actions do not; consequently, one should avoid binding oneself by promises or obligations that diminish the voluntary worth of an act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that what the law compels is less credited to the performer than to the exactor; he purposely makes promises uncertain and conditional to preserve freedom, and treats promises as morally weighty obligations which he seeks to avoid when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of large-scale innovation in politics (conservative principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great innovation and attempts to remake the foundations of a state commonly produce injustice and tyranny; to redress particular defects by universal upheaval risks worse evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses examples (Caesar's murderers, Pacuvius Calavius) and metaphors (surgeon who must replace flesh, not only cut away) to argue that tinkering, moderate correction, and respect for custom are safer than wholesale reform. He warns that 'all great mutations shake and disorder a state.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess government by maintenance and custom, not abstract ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: The best government for a nation is that under which it is maintained; form and convenience of government depend upon custom rather than imagined perfect polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Solon and Varro, Montaigne insists that one should prefer the government a people would accept and that reformers proposing ideal models appropriate perhaps to a new world are impractical for an established society. He counsels measuring against conditions below as well as above to find consolation.
